title: S1e4: MARQUEE MADNESS! Broadway Before the Tonys: What to See Spring 2026!
transcript: Up next on Broadway Broadcasting’s 5th Row Center, Marquee Madness. An opening-night frenzy on Broadway with 20 shows launching in five weeks. Why does this happen? Do we blame the Tonys, or is it something in the roots of theater business? And for audiences, the real question: when this many shows open at once, how do you decide what’s worth your time and your money? We’ve got some tips and secrets. Plus, I share the secrets behind previews, critics’ night, opening night, and how you can actually help shape a show. And later in BROADWAY unScripted, the spring surge unpacked. Predictions, frictions, and competitions. What our panel would see first. Welcome to Every Brilliant Thing and what they’d wait on and why. Join me. 5th Row Center. Broadway Broadcasting presents 5th Row Center, the secret to Broadway’s best seats in the house. Roma Torre, three-time Emmy Award-winning journalist and acclaimed theater critic, returns to television to reprise her signature theater reviews and exclusive insights. Plus, she brings us inside the 2025–2026 live theater season, and we bring you into the conversation with our exclusive live interactive roundtable. Subscribe to our YouTube channel for details. Join Roma in the best seat in the house. This is 5th Row Center. It’s that time of year when spring hits New York, the nights get brighter, and Broadway goes a little wild. Welcome to 5th Row Center. I’m Roma and Marquee Madness is descending on us. Spring brings one of the densest opening clusters of the season. Star vehicles, high-profile adaptations, revivals being reimagined, and a few real gambles. 20 major productions, all landing between March 12th and April 26th before Tony eligibility pressure peaks. And the first weeks make clear which shows you’re actually planning a night around and which you’re waiting to see pop up at TKTS. We are breaking down what’s opening and what’s worth watching. And it’s not just New York. Across the Atlantic, the West End is in its own spring surge with major openings, transfers, and revivals landing in quick succession. As springtime marks the end of the Broadway season in New York, the UK’s West End is blooming. The Prince Edward Theatre will be possessed by Beetlejuice, the musical adaptation of Tim Burton’s cult film on May 20th. And for fans of classic musicals looking to misbehave, Cole Porter’s High Society opens at the Barbican on May 19th, starring Helen George of Call the Midwife and Felicity Kendal. On May 2nd, Ava Pickett’s Tudor drama 1536 transfers to the West End following a critically acclaimed run at London’s Off-West End Almeida Theatre. Produced by Margot Robbie’s LuckyChap Company, the play tells the story of three ordinary women in Essex grappling with the fate of King Henry VIII’s second wife, Anne Boleyn. And speaking of, back here in the States, the musical about all of Henry’s wives, Six, wraps its run at Atlanta’s Fox Theatre through May 3rd. Disney’s 30th anniversary production of Beauty and the Beast moves in afterwards, running May 26th through the 31st. In Los Angeles, the Hollywood Pantages Theatre brings the national tour of The Sound of Music May 5th through the 24th, followed by Alicia Keys’ Hell’s Kitchen, opening May 26th. And at the Mark Taper Forum, Eboni Booth’s Pulitzer Prize-winning play Primary Trust arrives in LA for its regional debut. Back in the Northeast, Off-Broadway, the big arrival is New Born, running May 8th through June 8th at the Minetta Lane Theatre. Hugh Jackman stars in playwright Ella Hickson’s triptych of monologues alongside Sepideh Moafi, better known as Dr. Hashimi in HBO’s The Pitt, and Marianna Gailus. It joins Tom Noonan’s play, What Happened Was…, at the same theater, starring SNL’s Cecily Strong and Corey Stoll, currently running through June 14th. There’s a basic question I get all the time. What’s the difference between critics’ night, a preview performance, and opening night? Most people are surprised to learn critics do not review opening night performances. We’re invited earlier during designated press performances, which usually take place near the end of the preview period. My colleagues and I agree to an embargo and hold our reviews until a specific time, just after the official opening. Previews, the performances before opening night, remain a critical part of a show’s development. Although the way they’re used has evolved, during previews, the show continues to be developed in front of a live audience. Performances continue to settle, technical elements are refined, pacing adjusted, and audience response still matters because actors need a live audience to understand timing, rhythm, energy, and where, hopefully, applause unexpectedly breaks. That said, the show is often close to being complete by that point. In the past, many major changes happened during previews, and audiences would pay less for those pre-opening tickets. Today, shows are usually more fully formed in rehearsal spaces before they even reach the stage. And so, ticket prices are not reduced for those early performances. And by the time critics are invited, the shows are typically frozen. Directors generally won’t allow critics to attend until the work is ready to be judged. Another part of previews audiences don’t always see is how houses are filled. Shows need full audiences to function properly, and producers may give tickets away to insider groups and members of theatrical unions. It is a practice that is known as papering, and it helps to make sure that actors are playing to a full house. This entire system is relatively recent; inviting critics before opening night began in the 1970s. Before that, critics could only attend on opening night. And then they had to rush their reviews to meet same-night newspaper deadlines. My mother, who was a columnist, used to tell me about the stampede of critics racing out to payphones to make print that night. And that’s why critics traditionally are seated on the aisle. So, when you’re deciding when to buy tickets, it helps to know what you’re walking into. The closer to opening, the more likely you’ll see the polished version. But if you attend an early performance, you can always say you witnessed a show being born. Great stories, classic revivals, tales never told before, huge stars, unique stagings. We are in the grips of Marquee Madness. The rush is on as the Broadway season comes to a climactic ending in these last weeks of show openings. I am Roma once again, and these are the times that try theater insiders’ souls. Each year, we are traditionally bombarded in March and April by shows clamoring to make their marks and be fresh in the voters’ minds ahead of the Tony eligibility cutoff. 34 shows are competing for Tonys this season, but about half of them are opening in just these last weeks. From March 12th to April 26th, we are committed to seeing 16 Broadway productions. And that’s not even counting the new Off-Broadway offerings. So, joining us now to help sort it all out are a pair of veteran theater professionals who have literally seen it all: BroadwayWorld’s Richard Ridge and SiriusXM’s Julie James. Hey guys, how are you holding up? And you know, I don’t want people to be crying for us because, you know, boohoo, we’re seeing all these shows, but it can get exhausting, right? How’s it been for you, Julie? I know you’ve been running around a lot. It’s definitely dizzying, but it is, as we say, a champagne problem. Yeah, it gets to be a blur, doesn’t it? Richard, how’s it been for you? It’s a little crazy. We love what we do. It’s this time of year. We all know this, the March and April Madness, and it’s so exciting because there are so many brilliant things to see. So, let’s hear, what have been your favorites so far? And actually, I mean, I know we’re talking about the last six weeks, but there have been some really big, wonderful productions, and my favorite so far has been Ragtime. How about you guys? Ragtime is going to be such a big contender. This is such a beautiful new revival and a new production. It is stunning in every aspect, and boy, it’s so timely now with everything we’re going through. I mean, we all fell in love with Ragtime the first time around, but this production is just off the map, and the performances. I don’t know. They should just nominate everybody, right, Julie? I mean, everybody, absolutely flawless. That is just top form. But I also just worked with the cast of Chess in the SiriusXM studios. And as you know, someone who has known that score backwards and forwards since my days at conservatory, it’s really, it’s so bolstering that Chess is on Broadway and is enjoying a hit run after being a notorious flop that people have been dying, dying to fix. Anything else that surprised you in this latest season? An opportunity that I would call a little bit of a surprise. It has a lot of people talking: Titaníque. Titaníque coming to Broadway specifically to sort of pony into the Tony season is an interesting, and for some people surprising, choice simply because it ran in the New York area for, what was it, about three years? So you could argue that, you know, in terms of the local audience, most people that wanted to see it have seen it, and it is hilarious and clever and so much fun. Talk about what they’ve done with that show. Like you said, it was this small little musical that everybody fell in love with, and all of a sudden they just turned the volume up to like a million and just changed the cast and just, you know, blew it up for Broadway, which I think is so great. It is a surprise to me that the majority of productions this season are plays, not musicals. And I was doing a little bit of the math, but there are six new plays, four play revivals, four new musicals, and just two musical revivals. That’s in these last six weeks. That was a surprise. So why don’t we kind of take each one and look down the line based on the categories? And so let’s start with the new musicals. All right. Schmigadoon! It was the Apple TV series a couple of years ago, and it just really broke out and went mainstream. It wasn’t a cult TV show. Now it’s a big Broadway show. What do you anticipate with that one? And I think, Julie, you mentioned that you’re really excited about seeing it. Audiences are really looking for escapism, but they still want quality. And I think that has the potential for that. I enjoyed it when it was on Apple TV because it is a send-up of all the Golden Age musicals, and the writing was done in such a hilarious way where if you love those musicals, if you can name them, if you can catch the references, this is your show. And it’s just really fun to see how they sort of send up all of those old Golden Age musicals that we know and love and turn it into something that’s truly funny. Yeah, it’s a niche favorite, I would say. Yeah, Richard. Yeah, we’ve gone to the meet and greet. They presented five numbers. It was one of the most joyous rehearsal rooms to be in. This is what we, you know, escapism is what we need right now. You’re taking a family to the theater. You know, people wanted a big, splashy musical, and like I said, the Easter eggs are for anybody who’s ever listened to a cast album. You hear it. The characters are based on people we all love, and he did such a beautiful job putting this show together. It’s going to be joyous. Yeah. Ana Gasteyer, right? And Ann Harada. I’ve always loved them. Oh, they’re all in this show, right? And everybody, I mean, this is the best of the best working on Broadway right now in the musical theater genre, and they’re having the time of their life. They say it’s like going to summer theater camp when you first started out, you know, working on wanting to be an actor, whatever. They’re having the time of their life. Alex Brightman, Sarah Chase. All right. Beaches. This, too, is a show that I know has been in development for, gosh, I mean, at least a decade. The score of this show is incredible. It’s a beloved movie. The two leads in this show, I mean, Jessica Vosk, just like, you know, you could listen to her sing the phone book. The score is really, really beautiful. It’s Mike Stoller who’s doing this score, which just amazes me. The man is 93 years old. Yeah. And for anybody who doesn’t recognize the name, he made his mark with his songwriting partner Leiber. They were Leiber and Stoller, and they’re responsible for so many of the great Elvis Presley hits, Hound Dog and Jailhouse Rock, etc., etc. But I should also mention that, and this was a big deal to me, are they going to keep that iconic number that broke everybody’s hearts when we saw the movie, Wind Beneath My Wings? And yes, they are keeping the numbers. Last and certainly not least, the final show opening in this Broadway season is The Lost Boys. And there is great anticipation and excitement about that. And I don’t know really anything about it except I know it’s based on the film from, I think it was 1987. But I did hear a number from the show that was posted online, and it was just beautiful. It’s thrilling. We were in the rehearsal room, but now I have friends that have been teching at the theater. They fly. I mean, the whole look of this show is going to be mind-blowing, what they’ve done with this. The score is really great. Another incredible cast, and the three producers behind this all went to school together. So, I mean, they’ve been dreaming of putting this show together for a long time on Broadway. But I hear besides the incredible score and the book and the performances, the special effects of these vampire boys flying is going to be spectacular at the Palace. Yeah. Yeah. I’m really looking forward to that. And wow, what a way to end the season. Let’s move on quickly. The musical revivals. I can’t believe Cats is back, but in a very different form. It’s Cats: The Jellicle Ball. This is the only way I really need to see Cats. I don’t know. I don’t really need a literal, you know, production. I kind of feel the same way about Sunset Boulevard. It’s like, I don’t ever need the grand staircase and the turban again. It’s been taken to another level and did something really interesting with it. Oh, totally agree. It’s so beautifully crafted. So clever, what they’ve done. We’re all very excited about that. Yeah. And The Rocky Horror Show. I can’t believe they’re bringing that back. But again, you know, you’re right. The emphasis or the accent is on escapism, fun, funny stuff, and I guess that is the vibe that we’re all feeling these, you know, very difficult days in the world. So, I’m looking forward to that. It’s a really interesting cast, but for me, The Rocky Horror Show is about Sam Pinkleton, the director. I’m eager to see what, you know, fresh off of his Tony win for Oh, Mary! last season, for him to come back with a musical that’s so well-known and beloved. I’m interested to see what Sam Pinkleton is doing with Rocky Horror. That’s what’s in it for me. And Luke Evans said he cannot wait to put those Frankenfurter heels on and everything else. But, like Julie said, it’s all about Sam’s vision and everything else and the cast he has put together, just of every different element of actors. It’s really going to be spectacular. All right, let’s move on to the new plays because there are a bunch of them. Every Brilliant Thing, Giant, Dog Day Afternoon, Becky Shaw, The Fear of 13, and The Balusters. Now, Every Brilliant Thing opened March 12th, and so I think we all saw it, and I was just dazzled by it. I thought it was such a wonderfully original and engaging and heartwarming piece of work. And very special mention to Daniel Radcliffe, who just nailed it. He was wonderful. That was a big surprise to me. I didn’t expect it to be that thrilling. Welcome to Every Brilliant Thing. It’s so interesting to watch everybody in that house because Daniel starts at half hour wandering through the house, up to the balcony, up to the mezzanine, to give people little Post-its to talk about during the show. It’s one of the best feel-good things I’ve seen this season. I think Daniel is just exquisite in this. The subject matter is a little heavy, but it’s done in a beautiful light and so beautiful way, and everybody walks out of that theater feeling so much better. Yeah, it’s absolutely right. Yeah, I couldn’t agree more. If you need to feel a little better about life, go to that show, and really, a big portion of the audience gets to be in it. I mean, as you mentioned, Richard, including yours truly. I was there the night you were there. Oh, that’s right, Richard. Well, this is, I’ve never been so boldly insulted to my face and yet I loved it because Daniel ran up to me and my hubby sitting there, and we were on the aisle, and he said, he kneels down and he says to us, you know, rather quietly, “I would like you to play my old couple.” And I was like, “Your old couple?” I was like, “Yeah, sure.” You were asking Daniel. “We’ll be your old couple.” Anyway, it was a blast. We just really enjoyed it. Everybody leaves with a smile. They have the best time leaving that show. And to see him live. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And your chance to be in a Broadway show is always, you know, a little perk. All right. That’s your resume, Roma. You can add that to your resume. You know, I started out as an actress. I’ve never acted so much since I left. Anyway, Giant. Let’s talk about Giant. John Lithgow. This was the play that won the Olivier Award. And there’s just a great anticipation for it. I don’t know if it’s going to do as well on this side of the pond, but it does have a stellar crew behind it. Have you seen it? I know you were on the red carpet, Richard. Have you seen it yet? I’ve seen it. I think he is giving, this is gonna be the hardest category: best male in a play this year. He is incredible in this show. Everybody is, but John Lithgow is giving one of those career-defining performances. It’s like the Hamlet, King Lear. He is just bombastic and brilliant, and it’s selling incredibly. So, if you want to see some really great acting and one of our greatest, I think this is his 25th, could be his 26th Broadway show. He is so thrilled to be back. But he is a giant in this playing Roald Dahl. So timely now with everything that’s, you know, what he did at that time period. Another, like, you know, a wonderful piece that’s so timely, but brilliant performance. You know, correct me if I’m wrong, he’s 80 years old? Yes. And he’s in his prime. Isn’t that just incredible? Isn’t that incredible? It just blows me away. Dog Day Afternoon, this one I’m extremely excited about because who doesn’t love the film? And it’s got Jon Bernthal and Ebon Moss-Bachrach, right, from The Bear. I met them at the meet and greet, these two guys together. I mean, look at them. They are having Broadway debuts. They’re having the time of their life working on this. And Stephen was there that day and Rupert Goold, the director. The set is mind-blowing. The bank turns, and I love this movie. And this is going to be gritty. It’s Stephen Adly Guirgis. These people are introducing a whole new audience to the theater. It’s that gritty New York story. It’s very raw and very profane, but in the most entertaining fashion. Becky Shaw, what caught my eye, as having been raised in Pittsburgh, is Patrick Ball, who plays Dr. Langdon in The Pitt. Are you guys familiar with it at all, Julie? I didn’t see it before. So, I am looking forward to being introduced. And you make a great point about, you know, we have several stars from The Bear, The Pitt. People are drawn to the theater to see some of these favorites live and on stage without a net, as I like to say. Becky Shaw was a great show Off-Broadway at Second Stage, and now it’s getting its Broadway debut again. Really, really wonderful. Trip Cullman is directing that. Kelli O’Hara, Rose Byrne, Fallen Angels. I can’t wait to see that. But, like, you see Kelli in a play. Yeah. Yeah. Right. She’s so good no matter what she does. Kelli, I’m calling my trifecta because I work with the Metropolitan Opera at SiriusXM as well, and she’s been on stage at the Met Opera a number of times in recent seasons. Of course, she’s beloved on Broadway and in concerts. And now she’s doing a play on Broadway. So she’s infiltrating all of my worlds, and I love it. This is one of the most unknown Noël Coward plays because, I mean, these women are scandalous and everything else. It’s directed by Scott Ellis. Another stellar cast. Another TV favorite making their Broadway debut: Mark Consuelos. Oh yeah. And he was talking very lovingly about that cast in the studio, telling me about it recently. Oh yeah. He’s so excited because you had him in the studio. I had him in the rehearsal room. He’s like, it’s blowing my mind. I can’t believe this. In with Scott Ellis and Kelli O’Hara and Rose Byrne and all these people doing a drawing-room comedy. All right. Well, and Mark’s son is in Death of a Salesman making his Broadway debut. So, his son and father are making Broadway debuts side by side in the same season. How cool is that? You need Kelly Ripa then. That’s why all you need is Kelly to do something next and you’ll all be on stage. Let’s finish with the original plays, The Fear of 13. Adrien Brody and Tessa Thompson making their Broadway debuts. It’s a true story about a death row inmate who was innocent but spent more than two decades in prison. This one I’m very excited about because you know I love heavy drama, and Lindsey Ferrentino wrote the script of this. I mean, it’s a true story, you know, so this is going to be great. And then The Balusters. This one is David Lindsay-Abaire, right, who wrote Kimberly Akimbo and has that kind of quirky humor. That’s going to be a lot of fun. All right, let’s move on among the play revivals. Wow. Talk about some heavy hitters here. Death of a Salesman, with Nathan Lane and Laurie Metcalf and Joe Mantello directing. This is going to be seismic, I have to expect. I can’t wait to get into the Winter Garden Theatre to see this. I hear all these incredible things, that all my friends have gone and say it’s mind-blowing what Joe Mantello has rethought with Death of a Salesman and this cast, including the two boys who play Happy and Biff. I mean, Mr. Abbott and Ben Ainsworth. I mean, they’re all supposed to be wonderful in this. It’s all been shifted to another time period, right, Julie? Takes place, I think, in the ‘60s now, if I’m right. Yeah. And you can really expect, I mean, this is truly about the American dream, and we keep going back to the timeliness. You know, if you think about the 1960s, the promise of America, and then if you think of the promise of America in 2026, and to see it under the helm of Joe Mantello, but with the giants of Nathan Lane and Laurie Metcalf, it’s sure to be Winter Garden box office gold. And you know what I had heard was that Joe Mantello had some exclusive access to Arthur Miller’s writings for the play. So, we’re going to get a whole new dimension, I think, even without changing the setting. I think we’re going to understand the play even more so, which is hard to believe because I think it’s a perfect play. All right, Proof. Proof is back, and you know, I didn’t realize, I’m looking at my notes here. I think it opened 25, 26 years ago. I feel like I saw it only a couple of years ago. Oh, 25. I feel old. You’re a kid. Look at this cast with Don Cheadle and, oh, speaking of The Bear, Ayo Edebiri, right? This should be fun. And last I heard, the Obamas are producing this or putting their names and putting their money where their mouths are, which I think is so smart. Tommy Kail is directing this, and it won the Pulitzer Prize. Pulitzer. Yeah. Fallen Angels. We mentioned it. Yes. I really am thrilled to see Rose Byrne and Kelli O’Hara together on stage. I know we talked about it, but this should be, Aasif Mandvi, who makes me laugh just with his presence on stage. So that should be fun. And then finally, Joe Turner’s Come and Gone. Debbie Allen directing. She’s putting it again through a different lens, and it’s that August Wilson classic. I didn’t realize this is its third outing on Broadway. It’s a very popular play, and why not? It’s just the writing is just beautiful. Everybody is loving working with Debbie. They’re just having the time of their life working with her. They say the room, she prods and she’s like, I want you to be the very best. But then she pulls back. It’s that dancer thing. You know, the cast was telling me that she’s like, you know, you can go further. Go further. Go further. Trust yourself. Taj, all these people are just, you know, because she has the biggest history with the Allen sisters because they had a scholarship that she won when she was young, young, young, and so Debbie and the Allen sisters have been with her career forever, and she cannot wait to make her Broadway debut in this. Taraji is Taraji P. Henson, right? Making her Broadway debut, as well as Cedric the Entertainer, another Broadway debut. So we have all of these plays, you know, with a lot of individual actors showing up for a Broadway debut this season. It’s pretty marvelous. I wouldn’t call it unprecedented because I haven’t done that math, but it’s just a lot, a lot of very famous actors all making Broadway debuts in the same season. I’m just looking at the three other play revivals that opened earlier in the season. Also, they’re going to give everyone a run for the money: the three guys in Art, and every one of them, you know, could be a contender. And Oedipus, Mark Strong, who I’m in love with, that actor. I think he’s so wonderful. Waiting for Godot. Remember that? Oh, Keanu Reeves. Yeah, there’s been so much happening that all feels like ancient history, but it was only a couple of months ago. Well, you know, it explains also why all these shows wait till the last minute to open, because they want to be fresh in the voters’ minds. Richard, Julie, I just can’t thank you enough for your contributions. You have been wonderful on this edition of BROADWAY unScripted. Our next live taping time will be posted on our website, 5thRowCenter.com. And also, be sure, everybody, to subscribe to our YouTube channel. Until then, everybody, thanks. Thanks, Roma. Thanks for having us. Finally, this episode, the iconic marquee lights of Broadway are designed to do one thing: grab your attention. They sell shows, announce stars, and compete for your eye block after block. But for decades, those same lights have also been used quietly to acknowledge loss. When someone who matters deeply to the theater community dies, Broadway honors them in the simplest way it can, by turning those lights off. Usually within a day of the passing, just before performances begin that evening, the marquee lights dim for a minute. There is no announcement inside the theater, no speech, just a brief pause. I’ve witnessed this moment many times, and it never feels routine. What audiences may not realize is that this tradition isn’t set in stone. Broadway isn’t one institution. Each theater is independently owned, and participation has always been voluntary. It became controversial in recent years when, on the same night, some Broadway marquees went dark while others stayed lit, revealing that not every theater was participating in the tribute and prompting public debate about who’s included and who decides. It led to a shift behind the scenes. The Broadway League stepped away, and responsibility then moved fully to the theater owners themselves. Today, audiences usually learn about dimmings through press notices or by noticing the lights going out in real time. In a business built on visibility, it’s a very powerful gesture that the lights stop competing. The marquees all go dark only for a brief moment, but the pause and what it represents stays with you, and then the shows go on. We’ll leave it there for now. For more content, including the full BROADWAY unScripted roundtable, please subscribe to our YouTube channel at 5th Row Center, and subscribers will be notified when we host our next live roundtable so you can join in. From 5th Row Center, I’m Roma. Thanks for watching.
classificationReason: Panel discussion previewing 20 shows launching in spring 2026 with no single show as the focus. Brief mention of Every Brilliant Thing among many others.
